entities.summary: Johann (Hans) Schiltberger was a German traveller and writer born of a noble family, probably at Hollern near Lohhof halfway between Munich and Freising, around 1380. He was born into a wealthy family and received a good education, but his life took a dramatic turn when he was captured by the Mongols in 1408 during the Ottoman-Mongol invasion of Eastern Europe. After his captivity, Schiltberger spent several years in the court of Timur, also known as Tamerlane, in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, where he learned the Persian language and converted to Islam. He later returned to Europe, visiting the courts of the Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund and the Sultan of Hungary, and became a prominent figure in the intellectual circles of his time. Schiltberger's travelogue, 'The Travels of Johann Schiltberger', provides valuable insights into the politics, culture, and history of the medieval period, including the Mongol Empire's expansion and the rise of the Ottoman Empire. His experiences also reflect the complex dynamics of religious tolerance and cultural exchange in the medieval world. Schiltberger's legacy can be seen in the modern-day cultural heritage of the regions he visited, with his travelogue remaining a significant source for historians and scholars.
